passage: Thursday. Ajji is in the hospital and I did not want to talk today. At lunch I just stared at my roti while the other girls chattered. Uma sat down next to me and did not ask a hundred questions. She only said, "I'm here if you want," and pushed half of her banana chips toward me. We sat on the bench under the neem tree until the bell rang. She did not say it will all be fine, which is good, because I do not know that. I told her about the smell of the hospital at the very end, and she just nodded. I felt a little lighter. Jaya.

qa.q: What did Uma share with Jaya at lunch?
qa.a: She pushed half of her banana chips toward Jaya.

qa.q: Why was Jaya glad Uma did not say it will all be fine?
qa.a: Jaya does not know whether it will be fine, so hearing it would not have felt true or helpful.

qa.q: How could Jaya let Uma know the sitting together helped?
qa.a: Jaya could thank Uma simply and let Uma sit close again, since Uma's quiet presence was what Jaya needed. 😊

qa.q: What might Uma have been thinking as she sat quietly beside Jaya?
qa.a: Uma may have been unsure what to say and decided that staying close and not pressing for answers was the kindest thing.

grounding: A friend whose grandmother is ill is met with quiet company and a shared snack rather than questions or false reassurance.

passage: 'Pooja, you say Meenu hardly spoke all day because her grandmother is in hospital? Come, your Zeenat Khala will tell you what I learned at your age. My friend Farida went silent for a whole week once. Her grandmother, who lived with them, was very ill. Everyone kept saying, "Don't worry, she'll be fine!" and Farida just shrank smaller. I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing. I sat next to her under the jamun tree at recess and shared my aloo paratha, half and half, every day. On Friday she suddenly started talking about her grandmother's songs. I only listened. Years later Farida told me that in that week, I was the only one who didn't make her pretend.'

qa.q: What did young Zeenat share at recess?
qa.a: Her aloo paratha, half and half.

qa.q: How did young Zeenat feel about not knowing what to say?
qa.a: Unsure and awkward, but she chose to stay close quietly rather than say something empty.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Farida most?
qa.a: Sitting with her and sharing food without pushing questions or saying it would be fine, then just listening.

qa.q: How did 'Don't worry, she'll be fine!' feel to Farida?
qa.a: It made her shrink smaller; she felt she had to pretend instead of being allowed to be sad.

grounding: An aunt recalls sitting quietly with a friend whose grandmother was ill, being a kind presence rather than offering empty reassurance.

passage: It was sports day, and the sun blazed over the ground. Loudspeakers crackled, and the whole class cheered for the relay. Only Ankita sat on the steps, knees pulled up. That morning she had told Sonali in one sentence, 'Nani's in the ICU.' Then nothing more. Sonali's team needed her for the sack race in ten minutes. She looked at the queue, then at Ankita. She told her captain she'd be back in time and sat down beside Ankita with her packet of peanut chikki. She broke it in half and held one piece out. Ankita took it. Sonali didn't ask questions or say it would be fine. They just watched the relay together. When the whistle blew for the sack race, Ankita whispered, 'Go. Thanks for sitting.'

qa.q: What did Sonali share with Ankita?
qa.a: Her packet of peanut chikki, broken in half.

qa.q: Why did Sonali sit down beside Ankita despite the race?
qa.a: She felt concerned and caring for Ankita, whose Nani was in the ICU, and didn't want her to sit alone.
She shared food and stayed close without pressing with questions or promising things would be fine.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt with Sonali beside her?
qa.a: Less alone and grateful; she took the chikki and thanked Sonali for sitting.

grounding: On a busy sports day a girl sits quietly with a friend whose grandmother is very ill, sharing a snack and not pushing.
